@claude How long do you have to register a death in England, and does it have to be done in the district where she died?

In England you generally have 5 days to register a death. Hammersmith & Fulham's council page words it as 5 days from when the register office receives the medical certificate. The clock can differ if a coroner is involved, so ask the registrar if that applies. I couldn't open GOV.UK directly, so I'm relying on council pages for this.

It doesn't have to be in the district where she died, but it's quicker if it is. In another area you make a "declaration" at a local register office, and the office where she died completes the registration. You usually don't get certificates on the day, according to [Lambeth](https://www.lambeth.gov.uk/births-deaths-ceremonies-and-citizenship/deaths-and-funerals-sub-site/register-death/where-register) and [Salford](https://www.salford.gov.uk/births-marriages-and-deaths/register-a-death). If you need certificates quickly for the funeral or banks, register in the death district if you can.

Sources: [Hammersmith & Fulham](https://www.lbhf.gov.uk/births-deaths-and-marriages/deaths/how-register-death), [Norfolk](https://norfolk.gov.uk/42548), [Marie Curie](https://www.mariecurie.org.uk/information/grief/register-a-death)

@claude Do banks in England accept photocopies of a death certificate, or do they need certified copies?

It depends on the bank, so a plain photocopy isn't a safe bet. Santander says it accepts the original, a certified copy or a photocopy. Lloyds and Bank of Scotland want the original or a certified copy. Lloyds will copy and certify it in branch if you bring the original. Charter Savings Bank takes copies but prefers ones certified by a professional. United Trust Bank wants originals only. So Ben's "ask the bank" is sensible after all. Check which banks she used and look at their bereavement pages before you rely on copies. Ten certified copies from the registrar should cover it. I only found bank guides, not a single official rule, and I didn't check how recent each page is.

Sources: [Santander](https://santander.co.uk/personal/support/customer-support/bereavement), [Lloyds](https://www.lloydsbank.com/help-guidance/customer-support/bereavement.html), [Bank of Scotland](https://www.bankofscotland.co.uk/helpcentre/bereavement/), [Charter Savings Bank](https://chartersavingsbank.co.uk/Help/Bereavement), [United Trust Bank](https://www.utbank.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/23213-Bereavement-guide-v2.pdf)

@claude Does Kingston register office charge for certified copies of a death certificate, and is it the same fee as ordering them later online?

Yes, Kingston charges. Its site gives £12.50 per certified copy, described as a statutory fee, and says the price is the same whether you buy copies at registration or later. So ordering 10 would be £125. I only saw this in search snippets and didn't open the pages, so check it with the registrar when Ben rings.

Ordering later from Kingston online is £12.50 as well, by card, with standard orders sent second class. A priority copy is £38.50. The General Register Office (GRO) also seems to charge £12.50 online, but more by phone or post. That figure is less certain, and I couldn't tell how current it is.

Copies are cheaper when bought at registration, since there's no postage wait. You may not need 10 either. Some organisations will accept a copy back or a scan, so it could be worth asking NatWest tomorrow.

Sources: Kingston council pages (kingston.gov.uk certificates and registering a death) and GOV.UK's certificate ordering guidance.
